anchors.fact: In the 1870s Cognac's vineyard (about 280,000 hectares) was the biggest single vineyard region in the world; the phylloxera louse was a disaster for it, and by 1893 it was down to 40,000 hectares (Oxford COGNAC pdf 545–546; F1, F4).
anchors.meaning: A real crisis, with hope running out. No year for the louse's arrival (C7).
anchors.speaksTo: steps in when hope is running out

anchors.fact: It took more than ten years to find a rootstock that would grow in the region's deep chalk, and it came from Texas (Oxford pdf 545; F2).
anchors.meaning: Not a lucky save: a long search for the one answer that would hold on this ground.
anchors.speaksTo: a plan from long, patient knowledge

anchors.fact: From 1876 T. V. Munson collected American grapes out of Denison, Texas (over his life, more than 50,000 miles); the French wine industry, knowing his expertise, asked him for rootstock, and he sent it. The Handbook credits his work and Hermann Jaeger's. In 1888 a French delegation came to Denison to honour him (*Handbook of Texas*, secondary; M3, M5–M7).
anchors.meaning: Knowledge he gathered for its own sake (his word for the trips: passion) became the answer when the call came. Shared credit, always: Jaeger named. **Never** "Munson saved Cognac": no page ties him to Cognac's chalk (C1).
anchors.speaksTo: turns fear into a plan; gifts that count when they protect

anchors.fact: The vines were saved by grafting: European grapes grown on American roots (Oxford pdf 545 "a rootstock"; Handbook M5).
anchors.meaning: Saved by being changed: what grows above stayed, what holds it up is new.

anchors.fact: The region's floral grape, Folle Blanche, didn't suit grafting: its bunches grew so tight they were prone to rot. Ugni Blanc, with far less scent, replaced it (Oxford pdf 545–546; pdf 139 "fragile and hard to graft"; F3, F6).
anchors.meaning: The price the rescue itself brought: the unintended result of a save that worked. Never "it couldn't take the graft" (C3), never "lost" (C4).
anchors.speaksTo: the friend they could not save; fear: unintended results

anchors.fact: Cognac stands: the vineyard doubled to 110,000 hectares by 1976, and today about 76,000 hectares on the best chalk make it France's biggest vineyard given to one product (Oxford pdf 546; F5).
anchors.meaning: What was saved is bigger than what gave way. Never "restored" or "all brought back" (C8).
anchors.speaksTo: because of them, things that would have been lost are still here

anchors.fact: Folle Blanche is still grown: about 5% of Armagnac, its spirit floral and fruity, best young; it is a parent of Armagnac's baco blanc, and cognac may still be made from it (Oxford pdf 139; *Joy* pdf 419; F6–F8).
anchors.meaning: The hopeful turn for the proposal: once it's safe, there's room again for what the rescue had to leave behind. "Gave way in Cognac", not "gone".

anchors.fact: Ugni Blanc is a plain wine grape, but in Armagnac it gives an elegant spirit with body that ages well (Oxford pdf 139, 931, 879; F10).
anchors.meaning: The trade was a good one: the reading never calls the cognac or its grape dull.
anchors.speaksTo: gift: owns the trade so nobody else has to

anchors.fact: One of Folle Blanche's names in Gascony means "lip-stinger", which suggests how acidic it is; its spirit is floral and fruity, best young (Oxford ARMAGNAC pdf 139). Straight spirits carry minimal acid (*LI* pdf 140).
anchors.meaning: The brandy keeps the flower and loses most of the sting; ours gives a sharp edge back from another fruit. Never "the still leaves it behind", never "named for its sharpness" (audit v1 H4, H5).

anchors.fact: The *Flavor Matrix* lists gooseberries among the substitutes for grapes, and says grapes have an affinity for sour flavours (pdf 140).
anchors.meaning: A fruit that can stand in for the grape brings back the edge. A fruit's sharpness, never "the grape's own acid" (*Are You Quite Sure?*) (audit v1 H6).
anchors.speaksTo: the twist tied to the story

cocktail.closingLine: Keep the quarter of Folle Blanche, however small it looks. Once it's safe, find a place again for what you had to give up.
cocktail.glassware: old-fashioned glass (rocks glass, about 300 ml), one large ice cube
method: Make the syrup ahead: blend the gooseberries and sugar until smooth, with no heat. Press the purée through a fine sieve with the back of a spoon and keep the liquid.
Put the large cube in the old-fashioned glass to chill it.
Pour the cognac, then the Folle Blanche Armagnac, then the syrup, into a mixing glass or a jar. Fill it with ice cubes and stir for about 20 seconds, until the outside feels cold.
Strain it over the large cube. No garnish: the Folle Blanche's flower is the scent on top.
cocktail.name: Worth the Trade

recipe.note: made mostly from Ugni Blanc, the grape that replaced Folle Blanche once the vines were saved

recipe.item: young Armagnac made from Folle Blanche
recipe.note: look for "Folle Blanche" on the label, young or unaged, 40% or stronger. The grape that made way in Cognac and is still grown in Armagnac. If you can't find one, any young Armagnac gives the same balance, but it may hold little or none of the Folle Blanche

recipe.item: *for the syrup:* 200 g green gooseberries (fresh, or frozen and thawed), 100 g white sugar
recipe.note: blend cold until smooth, press through a fine sieve; keeps about a week in a closed jar in the fridge. Not cape gooseberries (physalis): a different fruit

cocktail.tagline: You know what has to change to save what matters.

reading.epigraph: Cognac was replanted on a rootstock from Texas. The grape that couldn't follow is here too.
whoYouAre: Something is going under: a friend's business losing money every month, a plan for a big day that has come apart, a team about to lose the thing it built. Everyone else is afraid of making it worse, so nobody touches it. You're the one who says, quietly, "this is what has to change." Then you see it through, step by step, until it stands again.

Afterwards, while the others are relieved, a part of you isn't, quite. Something had to give so the rest could hold: the old name over the door, the bigger room, the side of the project someone loved most. It worked, and you still think about that part. What you fear is what it might do that you didn't mean. It's why people trust you with the change: you weigh what it will take before anyone else thinks to ask, then you make the call anyway, and carry it yourself. Because of you, things that would have been lost altogether are still here.
yours: In the 1870s, the vineyards around Cognac were the biggest vineyard region in the world. Then a louse called phylloxera arrived, and by 1893 six hectares in every seven were gone.

The way out took over a decade to find: a rootstock, found in Texas, that could grow in Cognac's deep chalk, with the French vines grafted on top. The vineyard was saved by being changed. But one grape couldn't make the change. Folle Blanche, the region's floral grape, didn't suit grafting: its bunches grew so tight that they rotted. So Cognac planted Ugni Blanc, with far less scent, and made fine cognac from it all the same. The save was real, and much bigger than what gave way.

I like to think whoever chose the new roots knew what they were giving up, and chose it anyway, because the alternative was nothing at all. That's the call you make. Better still, Folle Blanche never disappeared. It made way in Cognac, but further south, in Armagnac, it's still grown, and its brandy comes out floral and fruity, at its best while it's young.

The cocktail I've made for you starts with cognac, from the grape that came through, and gives the other one its place back, as a nod to the part you had to let go: a smaller pour of young Armagnac made from Folle Blanche, a quarter of the brandy. In Gascony one of its names means lip-stinger, which hints at how sharp it is. Its brandy keeps the flowers but very little of the sharpness, because spirits carry almost no acid. So I've put some back with a syrup of green gooseberries, a fruit that can stand in for grapes in cooking. It's built like a great Old-Fashioned, and it comes out bright and fragrant: two brandies, with a green, sharp edge.

Once you've pulled something through and it's safe again, look for whatever had to make way. More often than you'd think, it hasn't gone anywhere, and now there's room. Bring a little of it back in, and let yourself enjoy the whole of what you saved.
